title: Training system
what: How the vine's permanent wood is laid out, chosen once at planting: Einzelpfahl ties arched canes to one stake per vine; Guyot lays a new cane along a wire each winter; Cordon keeps a permanent arm of short spurs.

steps: each needs about 1 m² of leaf per kg of fruit to ripen it fully
so ripeness follows bud load and canopy work, not the system's name
sources: canopy-and-yield.md#2.2 Leaf area to fruit ratio

choose: Einzelpfahl is the steep Mosel tradition. On workable land, Cordon spurs mechanise more easily but establish slower; Guyot canes need skilled hands but keep buds 4–10, more fruitful than basal buds in many vinifera varieties. Côte d'Or rules allow both, at most 8 buds per vine.
exam: Expect 'explain why steep sites use single stakes' or 'compare cane and spur pruning'. Link site → system → labour, cost and ripening; name the region.

check.question: Block B: 58 % slate; the Plot allows Einzelpfahl or Guyot. At the same bud load and leaf area, how do the two differ?
options: Both are hand-picked and ripen alike: leaf area per kg of fruit decides ripening
Guyot can be machine-harvested because its fruit hangs on a wire
Einzelpfahl ripens better: each vine has its own stake and more sun
Guyot needs far fewer hours because the wire does the tying
check.answer: Both are hand-picked and ripen alike: leaf area per kg of fruit decides ripening
check.why: 58 % is beyond machines whatever the trellis, so the hand work comes from the slope, not the stake. A stake opens the fruit to sun and air, but at equal leaf area per kg both ripen alike.

sources: canopy-and-yield.md#2.2 Leaf area to fruit ratio
law.md#Rules that bite in the simulation
simplification: Game simplification: labour follows the Plot's slope; the training system sets the maximum buds per vine, machine picking on flatter land and the planting cost. Bud fruitfulness by position is not modelled.
